sections.b: Paul reads Genesis 16 and 21 as an allegory: Hagar, the slave woman, stands for the covenant from Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, while Sarah, the free woman, stands for the promise and the Jerusalem above. The Gentile Galatians are Sarah's children, 'children born through the promise, as Isaac was.' He quotes Isaiah 54:1 and Genesis 21:10. The passage has been used well and badly; see the card at Galatians 4:21-31.

Paul calls Hagar the figure of the covenant from Mount Sinai, 'giving birth to children for slavery,' and says she lines up with the Jerusalem of his day (Galatians 4:24-25). The story of Genesis 16 and 21 tells it from Hagar's side: she is the first person in the Bible to name God ('the God who sees me', Genesis 16:13). The Plain notes that Paul's allegory has one purpose and does not tell her whole story.

sections.h: Sarah, the free woman and the barren one
sections.b: Sarah is the free woman whose son was born through the promise (Galatians 4:22-23), and Paul quotes Isaiah 54:1 ('Be glad, barren woman') as her song. The Jerusalem above is her counterpart, 'our mother' (4:26). Isaiah 51:2 already named Sarah as the mother of the people: 'Look at Abraham, your ancestor, and at Sarah, who went through labor to bear you.'

sections.h: Ishmael as the child of the flesh
sections.b: Paul says the son of the slave woman was 'born in the way of the flesh' and 'persecuted' the child born by the Spirit (Galatians 4:23, 29). Genesis says only that Ishmael was 'laughing' (Genesis 21:9); Jewish teachers read it as idolatry, immorality or violence (Genesis Rabbah 53:11). Paul applies the picture to the pressure on the Galatians, not to the descendants of Ishmael, and the rest of the Bible gives Ishmael a promise of his own (Genesis 17:20; 21:18).

Galatians 4:28 calls the Galatians 'children born through the promise, as Isaac was.' Paul uses Isaac as the pattern of a birth that depends on God's word, not on human effort, and says elsewhere that the promise is carried by Isaac, not by all Abraham's descendants (Romans 9:7-9). The point is not about biology: Isaac too was born to a body 'as good as dead' (Romans 4:19).

sections.h: Abraham's two sons, and Abraham's children
sections.b: In Galatians 4:22-31 Paul uses Abraham's household to ask who belongs to Abraham's family. The agitators, on his account, said it was a matter of circumcision; Paul says it is the promise, which came to Isaac and now to Gentile believers. This is the second half of an argument that began in 3:6-29. The Mishnah shows that the question of belonging was real in Jewish life: a convert whose mother was not an Israelite does not recite 'which the Lord swore to our fathers' when he brings first fruits, though in private prayer he may say 'God of the fathers of Israel' (Mishnah Bikkurim 1:4).

sections.h: Galatians 4:4-7: sent so that we might be adopted
sections.b: God sent his Son 'so that we would receive adoption as sons' (Galatians 4:5). Having made them sons, he sent 'the Spirit of his Son into our hearts,' who cries 'Abba, Father!' The child who is an heir is no longer a slave. Romans 8:14-17 says nearly the same, with 'we' crying out instead of the Spirit.

In these chapters the Spirit cries 'Abba, Father' in the hearts of believers (4:6), leads them so that they are not under law (5:18), opposes the flesh (5:17), and grows a single fruit in them (5:22-23). Believers are to walk by the Spirit (5:16), live by the Spirit and fall in line with the Spirit (5:25), and sow into the Spirit to reap eternal life (6:8). Paul gives the Spirit the work the agitators gave to the law.

sections.h: Two covenants, Sinai and the promise
sections.b: Paul says the women in Genesis stand for 'two covenants,' one from Mount Sinai and the other the promise (Galatians 4:24). He does not call them 'old' and 'new,' and he does not say the Sinai covenant is no covenant. Elsewhere he writes that the covenants belong to Israel (Romans 9:4) and that God does not take back his gifts and call (Romans 11:29).

Four things are said of the law in these chapters. Jesus was 'born under the law' (4:4). Those who want to be 'under the law' should listen to what it says (4:21). A circumcised man owes the whole law (5:3), and it is fulfilled in one saying, love of neighbor (5:14). And the Spirit-led are not 'under law' (5:18), and 'no law stands against' the Spirit's fruit (5:23). At the end Paul speaks of 'the law of Christ' (6:2).
sections.refs: Galatians 4:4-5; Galatians 4:21; Galatians 5:3; Galatians 5:14; Galatians 5:18; Galatians 5:23; Galatians 6:2

common: Paul does not say the Law of Moses is bad; he says it cannot give life or make Gentiles part of Abraham's family.
uncommon: Paul's 'not under law' (5:18) frees only Gentiles; Jewish believers remain bound to the Torah as a way of life (the view of scholars who read Paul within Judaism).

sections.h: Slavery as Paul's picture of the old life
sections.b: Galatians uses slavery for three conditions: the heir still a child (4:1-3), service to gods that are not gods and to the 'elements' (4:8-9), and the yoke of the law as a way to belong (4:24-25; 5:1). Paul then uses the same word for love: 'Through love, be slaves to one another' (5:13). The free woman and her children are set against the slave woman and hers (4:22-31).

sections.h: The Jerusalem above and the Jerusalem of today
sections.b: In Galatians 4:25-26 Paul sets 'the Jerusalem of today,' in slavery with her children, beside 'the Jerusalem above,' which is free and is 'our mother.' The idea of a heavenly Jerusalem is Jewish (2 Baruch 4:2-6; 4 Ezra 10), and Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2 use it too. Paul himself kept up the collection for the poor in the earthly city (Galatians 2:10; 6:10 is the same spirit).

Paul places Mount Sinai 'in Arabia' (Galatians 4:25), in line with Exodus 3:1 (Midian) and with his own journey to Arabia (Galatians 1:17). The sentence has a variant: some witnesses leave out 'Hagar.' For Paul, Sinai is the place of the law given to Israel, and the covenant given there is set beside the earlier promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:17).

Paul tells Gentile men that if they get circumcised Christ will not help them and they owe the whole law (Galatians 5:2-3). He says that in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any strength, but faith working through love (5:6), and that a new creation is what matters (6:15). He does not say that Jews should stop circumcising their sons; the charge that he 'still' preached circumcision (5:11) may rest on what people knew of him, such as his circumcising Timothy (Acts 16:3) or his earlier life as a Pharisee; the letter does not say what he taught before.

sections.h: Galatians 4:10: days, months, seasons and years
sections.b: Paul tells the Gentile Galatians, 'You are keeping close track of days, months, seasons and years' (4:10) and compares this to turning back to the 'elements.' The calendar may be Jewish (Sabbath, new moon, festivals, Sabbath year), or pagan. The churches read the verse differently where the weekly Sabbath is concerned; see the card.

Paul says the Galatians 'were slaves to beings who are not gods by their nature' (4:8), in the language of Israel's prophets against idols (Deuteronomy 32:21; Jeremiah 2:11). 'Idol worship' stands in the list of the flesh's works (5:20). He then ranks the return to the 'elements' with that old service.

Paul's 'allegory' in Galatians 4:24 is, most think, typology: a figure in Genesis has the same shape as a present reality. The two women, the two sons, the two mountains and the two Jerusalems are matched in columns. The pattern is not an unrestrained symbol hunt; it ties to the history of the household of Abraham.

sections.h: Paul's one use of the word 'allegory'
sections.b: The verb allegoreo occurs only in Galatians 4:24. Chrysostom, Calvin and others took it as a type or comparison. Philo of Alexandria had made Hagar the 'preliminary studies' and Sarah wisdom. The reader should compare how Paul uses the story with how Jewish and Christian writers used it.

Galatians 4:23, 28 and 31 speak of children 'born through the promise,' and Galatians 3:16 (see there) has argued that the promised offspring is Christ. The Gentile believers are children of the promise as Isaac was. Paul's argument turns on the contrast between birth by promise and birth by the flesh, not on descent.

Paul writes that God sent his Son, 'born of a woman, born under the law,' and never mentions a virgin birth, Mary or Joseph. Most scholars read the words as a statement of true humanity (compare Job 14:1). The churches read the silence differently; see the card at Galatians 4:4.

Galatians 5:4 warns those 'being justified by the law' that they have been cut off from Christ and fallen away from grace. In 5:5 the Spirit and faith wait with longing for 'the righteousness we hope for,' which some read as the final verdict on the last day. For the main statements of justification, see Galatians 2:16 and 3:11.

'Only faith has strength, faith working through love.' The sentence gives faith the action Paul denies to circumcision. Catholic teaching reads it as faith 'formed by love,' and the Reformation traditions as a faith that justifies alone and always acts in love. In the Spirit's fruit the same word returns, translated 'faithfulness' (5:22).

Paul tells those who seek to be justified by law, 'You have fallen away from grace' (Galatians 5:4). In popular English the phrase means a moral lapse; in Paul it means leaving the basis of grace for the basis of law. The letter ends with a blessing: 'may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit' (6:18).

sections.h: The whole law in one saying
sections.b: In Galatians 5:14 Paul says the whole law stands fulfilled in Leviticus 19:18, 'You are to love your neighbor as yourself.' Romans 13:8-10 says the same, and Jesus gave the command a central place (Matthew 22:39-40). Jewish teachers also called it a great principle of the Torah (Genesis Rabbah 24:7). Paul sets it against the quarrels of the Galatian churches, who were 'biting and devouring' one another (5:15).

Three passages bear on whether believers can fall: those 'being justified by the law' have 'fallen away from grace' (5:4); those who practice the works of the flesh 'will not inherit God's kingdom' (5:21); and the promise of harvest 'as long as we do not quit' (6:9). Catholic, Orthodox and Methodist teaching reads them as real warnings; Reformed teaching reads them as marks of those who never truly believed or as means God uses to preserve his people. See the card at 5:4.

sections.h: Porneia in the works of the flesh
sections.b: The first three works of the flesh are 'sexual immorality, uncleanness, shameless living' (Galatians 5:19). The Greek porneia covers a wide range of sexual behavior condemned by the law. The KJV's list adds 'adultery' from the Byzantine text, which is not in the older manuscripts. Paul says those who practice such things 'will not inherit God's kingdom' (5:21).

sections.h: Sorcery in the works of the flesh
sections.b: The Greek pharmakeia in Galatians 5:20 originally meant the use of drugs and later magic and spells, from which English gets 'pharmacy.' It stands between idol worship and hatreds in the list of the flesh's works. Revelation 21:8 and 22:15 use related words.

The agitators are named in Galatians 4:17 ('They are eager for you, but not for any good purpose'), 5:7-12 (the one who cut in front of you, the one who is disturbing you, who will carry the judgment) and 6:12-13 (the ones pressing circumcision, 'to keep from being persecuted because of the cross of Christ'). Paul describes their motives as pressure and show. Views of who they were are in the note at 5:10.

sections.h: Crucified with Christ's cross: the flesh, the world, and Paul
sections.b: Galatians 5:24 says those who are Christ's 'have crucified the flesh, with its passions and its desires.' Galatians 6:14 says Paul will boast only in the cross, 'through which I have been crucified to the world, and the world has been crucified to me.' The cross is also the stumbling block that Paul would have removed if he preached circumcision (5:11).

'Circumcision is nothing, and so is uncircumcision. A new creation is what matters.' The idea comes from Isaiah 65:17 and Jewish hopes for the world's renewal (Jubilees 1:29). Paul says it has begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). Here it replaces the circumcision distinction as the thing that matters.

Paul ends with a blessing on 'all who will walk by this rule, and on the Israel of God.' The phrase occurs nowhere else. It has been read as the church of Jews and Gentiles, as Jewish believers, or as the Jewish people. The deep dive and card on the chapter set out the readings and the churches' teachings.

'You who live by the Spirit should put that person back on his feet, with a gentle spirit.' The verb is the one for mending a net. Paul's instruction is to restore, not to expel; it goes with 'carry each other's heavy loads' (6:2). Matthew 18:15-17 gives a procedure; Paul gives the spirit.

In these chapters 'flesh' is used for ordinary human birth (4:23, 29), for a power opposed to the Spirit (5:16-17), for the works listed in 5:19-21, and for the circumcised flesh the agitators want to boast about (6:12-13). Those who belong to Christ 'have crucified the flesh' (5:24), and whoever 'sows into his own flesh' reaps decay (6:8).

'Christ has set us free, to live in freedom' (5:1) and 'You were called to freedom, brothers' (5:13). Freedom is from the yoke of slavery and the flesh, and for service: 'Through love, be slaves to one another.' The Hagar and Sarah story gives freedom its mother, 'the Jerusalem above' (4:26).

The agitators want to boast about the flesh of the Galatians (6:13), and Paul will boast only in the cross (6:14). Each person is to test his own work and then take pride in himself alone, not by comparison (6:4). The standard is Jeremiah 9:23-24.

In these chapters Paul speaks of his own weakness and the Galatians' welcome (4:13-15), becomes a mother in labor (4:19), claims to speak with his own hand in large letters (6:11), and says he carries the marks of Jesus on his body (6:17). The Galatians are urged to be like him (4:12) and not to trouble him further (6:17).

'Whoever sows into his own flesh will harvest decay from the flesh. Whoever sows into the Spirit will harvest eternal life from the Spirit.' This is the two ways in the language of the field: two seeds, two harvests. Job 4:8 and Proverbs 22:8 have the proverb; Paul applies it to flesh and Spirit.

sections.h: Galatians 4:13-15: Paul's illness as the Galatians saw it
sections.b: Paul tells the Galatians that he first preached to them 'in a weakness of the flesh,' a 'test' that they did not scorn, and that they would have given him their eyes (Galatians 4:13-15). Some readers link this to the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12:7, and the eye reference has led to guesses about eye disease; the large letters of 6:11 are sometimes added. Paul does not say what the illness was.

The warning that a circumcised man 'becomes a debtor, bound to do the whole law' (Galatians 5:3) gives the practical meaning of 'works of the law' for Gentile converts: it was the way a convert took on the Torah. Paul sets this against 'fulfilling' the law in love (5:14). See the earlier part of the letter for 2:16 and 3:10.

sections.h: Clues to the Galatian churches in chapters 4-6
sections.b: Chapters 4-6 give a few clues to the readers: they once served gods that were not gods (4:8), received Paul warmly in his illness (4:13-15), had teachers (6:6) and were quarreling (5:15, 26). The scene of the welcome 'like an angel of God' resembles the crowds of Lystra in Acts 14:11-13, which the South Galatian view stresses. The North Galatian view points to the Celtic region of Pessinus and Ancyra.

In Galatians 4:3 and 4:9 Paul speaks of 'the basic elements of the world' that kept humanity in slavery. One of several readings hears spirit powers of the sort named in Colossians 2:8, 20; others hear the physical elements, the ABCs of religion, or pairs of opposites. See the topic on the elements of the world.

Love is the way faith works (5:6), the way believers serve (5:13), the one saying that fulfills the law (5:14) and the first of the Spirit's fruit (5:22). The community's failure of love is named in the picture of biting and devouring (5:15).

sections.h: A possible echo of the collection (Galatians 6:10)
sections.b: Paul tells the Galatians to work for the good of everyone, 'above all for those in the household of faith' (6:10). The verse does not mention the collection; the link is only a possible echo. In the same letter he says the Jerusalem apostles asked only that he 'remember the poor,' which he was eager to do (2:10). The Galatian churches were among those asked to contribute (1 Corinthians 16:1).

sections.h: The 'elements of the world' in Galatians 4
sections.b: In Galatians 4:3 and 4:9 Paul says that before Christ his readers, and Jews as well as Gentiles in the 'we' of 4:3, were slaves 'under the basic elements of the world', and that going back to days, months, seasons and years (4:10) would be a return to 'weak and poor elements'. The Greek is stoicheia tou kosmou. Readings: the four physical elements; the ABCs of religion; spirit beings tied to the stars and elements; the pairs of opposites on which the old world stood; or any basic rules that bind a people before Christ. The verb systoicheo in 4:25 shares the root.
